title: Story Chains
note: Five stories told across a career in three or four beats each, from CONTENT_PLAN.md section 3: The Pilot (pilot_*), The Whistleblower (whistle_*), The Protégé (protege_*), The U-Turn (uturn_*) and The Bond (bond_*, scholars only). Each starts with an ordinary card; its choices set the flags the next beat reads, and the next beat is scheduled with inYears and a chance. Beats that may fall due after the player has moved on have alternates (a promotion, a move into politics, a move between ministries), and a beat that names the junior, the peer or the fellow MP checks the flags on that person. The Pilot's and the U-Turn's subjects come from the player's ministry (parts keyed by requires.ministry); a U-Turn beat for a player who has since moved ministry names the policy without guessing. Folder items and Declassified lines for these flags are in game.json (folder, declassifiedFlags).

events.body: Your division has the money for a one-year pilot of {scheme}, in three {scheme.place}, and you choose which three. If it works, the Minister will announce it in the Committee of Supply debate in two years, using the numbers your pilot produces. Where you run it will decide what those numbers look like.

choices.text: Pick the three likeliest to make it work.
choices.outcome: You pick three {scheme.place} with busy volunteers and short queues. The launch has a ribbon, a banner and a photographer, and the photograph goes upstairs captioned "Good start."

choices.text: Pick the three likeliest to make it fail.
choices.outcome: You pick the three {scheme.place} where schemes go to struggle. The launch is quiet. Within a month you know more about why things fail than anyone else in the building.

choices.text: Draw the sites by lottery, and hold half back as a control.
choices.outcome: A lottery picks three {scheme.place} to get the pilot and three more to go without, for comparison. The three without get a letter explaining why, and draw more complaints than the pilot does. Your results, though, will be very hard to argue with.

options.text: In the three {scheme.place} you picked, take-up was 71%. But page 40 of the evaluation points out that those three would have taken up almost anything.
options.a: 71% goes into the speech on its own, and the Minister reads it with feeling. The warning stays where it was: on page 40.
options.b: 71% goes up with its paragraph from page 40, and the speech keeps both: "in places that were already well served". No other line in the speech gets less applause.
options.c: The speech goes ahead without your pilot. You spend another year running it in ordinary {scheme.place}, not ones picked to like it. The number you get there is smaller, and you trust it.

options.text: In the three hard {scheme.place} you picked, take-up was 23%. For those three, that's remarkable. In a speech, without the context, it's just 23%.
options.a: You send the figure from the best of the three: 64%. It's true of that one. The speech doesn't say which one, and nobody asks.
options.b: 23% goes up with its context, and the speech uses both. The line gets no applause, and the Minister's office asks, kindly, whether there was a better number.
options.c: The speech goes ahead without your pilot. A second year in the same three brings take-up to 31%, which nobody upstairs asks about, and which you believe.

options.text: Compared with the three {scheme.place} that went without, the pilot raised take-up by four percentage points: a real gain, properly measured, and much smaller than anyone had hoped.
options.a: You send the gain in the pilot's best month: nineteen points. Every word is accurate. The speech says "up to nineteen points", and the Minister says it twice.
options.b: Four points go up with the paragraph explaining why four is good. The speech uses it. A newspaper calls the result "modest", and quotes your paragraph correctly.
options.c: The speech goes ahead without your pilot. A second year confirms the four points, and finds that they last. Nobody upstairs asks, and you write it up anyway.

events.body: Years ago, as a civil servant, you sent a flattering number from your pilot into a Minister's speech. The Auditor-General's report now traces an expensive shortfall in the national scheme to that number. {journalist} has found your name in the file, and wants a comment by six.

choices.text: Say the number was yours, and so was the choice.

choices.text: Say the ministry will respond in due course.

events.title: Forty-One Purchases
events.body: {junior} closes your door and opens a spreadsheet: forty-one purchases from one vendor, each between $5,900 and $5,999. Anything over $6,000 would have needed quotes from other vendors, so every one sits just under the line. All forty-one were approved by someone two floors up. {junior} wants to know what you'll do.

choices.text: Take it upstairs yourself, as your own finding.
choices.outcome: You send it up under your own name, retyped so that nothing points back to {junior}. Two floors up, someone stops saying good morning to you. {junior} thanks you once, and never mentions it again.

choices.text: Thank {junior}, and leave it where it is.
choices.outcome: You thank {junior} for being thorough, and say you'll keep an eye on it. That evening {junior} emails you a note of the meeting, for the record. You never reply, and after a month {junior} stops asking.

choices.text: Report it through the proper channel, naming {junior} as the source.
choices.outcome: The form has a box marked "Source", and {junior}'s name goes in it, as the form requires. Within a week the whole floor knows about the box, and who was in it.

events.title: The Review Panel

options.text: A few years ago {junior} brought you forty-one purchases kept just under the $6,000 line, and you reported them as your own finding, to protect {junior}. The case is closing: the vendor has been barred, and the officer two floors up who approved the purchases has quietly retired. The review panel wants to commend whoever first spotted the pattern, and {junior} is copied on its email.
options.a: Give the panel {junior}'s name.
options.aOut: The commendation goes to {junior}, in a paragraph that uses the word "diligence" twice. {junior} thanks you in the lift, and does not say whether {junior.they} wanted it.
options.b: Keep {junior}'s name out, as you did then.
options.bOut: The panel commends you, since the report went up under your name. {junior} replies all with congratulations, and is the first to clap at the townhall.

options.text: A few years ago {junior} showed you forty-one purchases from one vendor, each just under the $6,000 line, and you left it there. Now the Auditor-General has found them too, and a review panel wants to know when the ministry first knew. {junior} has already been interviewed, and kept the email.
options.a: Tell the panel you were shown them years ago.
options.aOut: The panel records the date, and the word "candour". Its paragraph on supervision is about you, without your name in it. {junior} is not called again.
options.b: Tell the panel you do not recall.
options.bOut: The panel records that you do not recall. It also has {junior}'s email, which recalls everything, with a timestamp. Nothing further is said to you in writing.

options.text: A few years ago you reported {junior}'s spreadsheet of forty-one purchases through the proper channel, with {junior} named as the source. It led to a barred vendor and a quiet retirement two floors up. It also left {junior}'s name in the Source box, where everyone two floors up could read it. In this year's ranking, {junior} is in the middle again, for the third year running.
options.a: Argue for {junior} in the ranking.
options.aOut: You argue for forty minutes and spend most of your goodwill. {junior} moves up four places and never learns why. Two floors up, someone notes who argued.
options.b: Let the ranking be. It was never about the report.
options.bOut: {junior} stays in the middle, where the ranking says the work is. You believe this. You would like to believe it slightly more than you do.

events.title: An Hour a Fortnight
events.body: At the end of your one-to-one, {junior} asks whether you would be {junior.their} mentor. Not the official scheme, with its forms and lunch vouchers: the real thing, an hour a fortnight, and the truth when {junior} needs it. You don't have the hours, and upstairs will judge you partly by how {junior} turns out.

choices.text: Yes: an hour a fortnight, and the truth.
choices.outcome: The hours are mostly about other people's papers, and once about {junior}'s. You say the true thing twice in the first year. {junior} writes both down, and argues with one.

choices.text: Yes, and give {junior} the hardest file in the division.
choices.outcome: You give {junior} the file nobody wants, and stand behind it. {junior} nearly drowns in it, then does not, and the people upstairs remember who chose {junior.them} for it.

choices.text: Say no, kindly. You do not have the hours.
choices.outcome: {junior} says {junior.they} understood, and plainly did. The hours you kept go into a paper that is very good. {junior} finds a mentor on the next floor, who has the hours.

events.title: In Front of Forty
events.body: A few years ago you agreed to mentor {junior}. Today, at the ministry's strategy retreat, {junior} stands up during your presentation and says, politely and with figures, that your paper's central assumption is wrong. {Junior} is mostly right. Forty colleagues, several of them senior to you, wait to see what you do.

choices.text: Concede the point, there and then.
choices.outcome: You say {junior} is right, and say why. The room relaxes. The paper is rewritten, better, with {junior}'s figures in it and {junior}'s name on the slide.

choices.text: Hold your line, and take it up with {junior} afterwards.
choices.outcome: You hold your line, smoothly, and the room moves on. Over kopi afterwards you concede most of it. {junior} accepts, and notes, without saying so, where each was said.

choices.text: Say you asked {junior} to make that point.
choices.outcome: "Exactly the challenge I asked {junior} to bring," you say, and the room is impressed with you both. {junior} smiles, and brings nothing to the next one-to-one.

options.b: The minutes record your view: "not yet". {junior} hears about it within the day, as everyone does, and is at the next one-to-one on time, with questions.

events.body: Nine MPs have filed Parliamentary Questions on one of your ministry's policies, {policy}, and you will give the replies in the House. Your officials' draft ends by saying the policy "remains under review", in square brackets: keep the phrase, or cut it? Whatever you say will be in Hansard, under your name, for good.

choices.text: Strike it. The policy is sound, and it stays.
choices.outcome: "The policy is sound, and it will stay." Hansard records it, and two newspapers print it as a pull quote. Your officials file the bracketed phrase, in case.

choices.text: Keep it. Say the policy remains under review.
choices.outcome: "Under review" satisfies the House and worries the officials who designed the policy, who ask what exactly you are reviewing. By Friday, you find that you are reviewing it.

choices.text: Strike the adjectives too. Answer with figures only.
choices.outcome: Your replies run to nine figures and no adjectives. Members find little to quote and no supplementary questions to ask. Hansard records the most accurate answers of the sitting, unread.

choices.text: Argue to keep it, from your own replies.

choices.text: Agree, and say it should go quickly.

choices.text: Propose a phase-out, so nobody has to say "reverse".
choices.outcome: The paper is amended: the policy will be "phased out" over six months, about as long as reversing it would have taken. Everyone agrees that this is different.

events.title: A Year Away
events.body: The Public Service Division offers to sponsor a master's degree for you: a year at {school}, with fees and an allowance paid. It comes with a bond of its own: two more years in the service, served after your scholarship bond ends. Leaving before then would mean paying back the cost, with damages.

choices.text: Go. Sign for the extra two years.
choices.outcome: Twelve months, officials from forty countries, and a seminar in which you are asked to explain Singapore. You come back with a master's, a bond that ends at thirty-two, and someone else in your old job.

choices.text: Decline. Your division needs you this year.
choices.outcome: Upstairs is grateful, in a way that lasts exactly one ranking cycle. The offer is not repeated. The division, it turns out, did need you, though not as much as it said.

choices.text: Do a master's part-time, at night, on your own money.
choices.outcome: Two years of evenings, $40,000 of your own, and not one year added to your bond. The degree is the same degree. Nobody at work asks about it, which was most of the point.

options.text: the two master's years included
for all the years left

events.body: You're still serving your scholarship bond, so leaving the service now means paying PSC damages for the years you haven't served. A bank wants you by March, and will pay those damages in full, {left}, and call it a signing bonus. Your bond deed was signed by you and by two sureties, usually family, who promised PSC you would serve it out.

choices.text: Let the bank pay. Resign in March.
choices.outcome: The bank's cheque matches the damages to the dollar. Your resignation is accepted in one line, and the farewell email from upstairs is warmer than you expected, and shorter.

choices.text: Decline. A deed is a deed.
choices.outcome: You decline in two lines, and keep the bank's letter in a drawer. The offer stands until June, when a younger officer takes it. You hear about that at a wedding.

options.b: You make the case for staying, with your own master's as Exhibit A. Your scholar stays, and asks, a month later, how one applies for the sponsorship.

options.b: You make the case for staying, and leave out the master's you turned down. Your scholar stays. The bank hires someone else by June, as banks do.

events.body: Years ago a bank offered to pay off your scholarship bond, and you said no. Since then PSC has made you a mentor to one of its scholars, now three years into a six-year bond. Your scholar asks to meet: a bank has offered to pay off that bond too, and wants an answer by Friday. Your scholar wants to know what you did.

choices.outcome: You say what nobody at PSC says: it is a contract, and the bank is paying. Your scholar resigns in March. PSC thanks you for your time as a mentor, in writing.

events.title: Your Old School
events.body: Years ago you turned down a bank that offered to pay off your scholarship bond, and served the bond in full. Now your old school has asked you, as a former student in Parliament, to talk to its final-year students about scholarships. The question they sent in most often, the principal writes, is about the bond.

choices.text: Tell them about the bank's letter, and why you said no.
choices.outcome: You tell them about the letter and the deed, and the hall goes quiet in the right way. Three students ask about the bank afterwards. One asks which bank.

choices.text: Tell them the bond is the best deal they will ever sign.
choices.outcome: You make the case, and it is a good one. The principal thanks you warmly. A student in the front row writes "best deal" on the back of a hand.

choices.text: Leave the bond out. Talk about the work.
choices.outcome: You talk about budgets, lifts and a scheme that failed properly, for forty minutes. The question about the bond comes anyway, at the end, and you answer it in a sentence.
